name: Bowlski
tagline: An iOS app for keeping bowling scores across players, games and league nights.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Bowling scoring is a closed rulebook: ten frames, two rolls, strikes and spares borrow from the next frames, tenth frame gets a bonus ball. There is no network, no proprietary data, no server that needs to exist. An agent can produce a working multiplayer scoresheet with correct pin math and persistent history in one sitting, and a PWA pinned to your home screen is close enough to a native app for a bowling alley. What you give up is the polish: haptics, a pin-picker that feels good with greasy fingers, and someone else having already fixed the tenth-frame edge cases. Test the tenth frame, that is where DIY builds always break.
coreLoopDIY: A local, installable web app that tracks 1 to 6 players through ten frames with correct strike, spare and tenth-frame bonus scoring, and saves finished games to a history list with averages.
requirements: A phone to install the PWA to the home screen
Willingness to hand-verify the tenth frame scoring against a real scoresheet
whatYouLose: Native feel: haptics, smooth animations, and a tap target designed for a dim bowling alley
App Store install and updates instead of an added-to-home-screen web page
Any iCloud sync between your phone and anyone else's
Whatever extras the paid app has bundled: league tracking, stats charts, share cards
Somebody else's already-debugged scoring edge cases
moatNotes: The only real advantage here is that the rules are already implemented correctly and the buttons feel nice under a thumb.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a few dollars once is less effort than an evening of work, and because a scorekeeper is only useful if it is already on your phone before the ball hits the lane. Nobody wants to debug frame-bonus logic while their turn is up. That is a completely reasonable purchase, it is just not a durable business moat.
notes: One of the purest one-shot candidates on the list: the spec is a rulebook you can look up in two minutes.
prompt:
Build a local-first bowling score keeper as an installable PWA. No accounts, no backend, no telemetry, no analytics.

Stack, non-negotiable: Vite + React + TypeScript, plain CSS (no UI framework), state persisted to localStorage. Single page app, no router beyond a simple view switch. No .env needed since there are no secrets.

Core features:
- New game setup: add 1 to 6 players by name, reorder, remove.
- Scoring input: for each player's turn, a pin-count keypad showing only legal values (0 through remaining pins) plus explicit X (strike) and / (spare) buttons.
- Correct ten-pin scoring: strike = 10 + next two rolls, spare = 10 + next roll, tenth frame allows a third ball when the first two earn it. Running totals update as soon as the bonus rolls are known, and show blank (not zero) until then.
- Undo last roll, always available.
- Classic scoresheet grid: per-frame boxes with the small roll marks and the cumulative total underneath, horizontally scrollable on a phone.
- Game end: winner highlighted, save to history.
- History view: list of past games with date, players, scores; per-player average, high game, strike percentage.
- Export all data as JSON, and import it back.

Explicitly out of scope: cloud sync, multi-device, league management, sharing images, ball/lane tracking, dark mode toggle (just respect prefers-color-scheme).

Mobile requirements: viewport meta with no zoom weirdness, tap targets at least 44px, works fully offline via a service worker, web app manifest with name, icons and standalone display so it installs to the iOS home screen.

Correctness: put all scoring logic in one pure module, scoreGame(rolls), with zero UI imports. Write Vitest tests for it covering a perfect 300 game, all spares (190), all nines-and-a-miss (90), an open-frame game, a tenth-frame spare with bonus ball, and a game in progress with pending bonuses. Tests must pass before you consider it done.

Deliver a README with npm install, npm run dev, npm run test, npm run build, and one line on how to install it to a phone home screen from the local network.
